summary:
Madhya Pradesh has no state-specific transgender statute and no documented state-level enforcement series. Legal uniformity across the country sets the deviation at ±0.02, so a visitor to Madhya Pradesh is assessed against the national framework rather than any provincial rule.

That framework was altered on 25 March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The amendment replaces the self-identification route affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014 with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition now rests on medical certification. The amendment makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery and conditions identity recognition on medical certification, a direct documents consequence for a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. The bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The scoring deviation for Madhya Pradesh is ±0.02 against the national score, reflecting legal uniformity across states rather than any measured difference in local conditions.

No Madhya Pradesh-specific protest, arrest, checkpoint incident or police conduct is sourced. The demonstrations recorded against the March 2026 amendment took place in Mumbai, and the checkpoint abuses documented in 2024 occurred at a railway station in Kolkata, in Railway Protection Force custody in Assam, and at Chennai International Airport — each a single data point illustrating a national pattern of friction at screening points, not evidence of conditions inside Madhya Pradesh.

Official and critical readings of the March 2026 amendment diverge sharply. The government frames it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; rights groups and activists frame it as exclusion and criminalisation. The sources do not reconcile these positions.

The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines bind police and education authorities in Tamil Nadu, not Madhya Pradesh, so their direct reach does not extend here; their value to a visitor lies in establishing that high courts have been willing to intervene. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 is a national assessment and is not broken down by state.
localsOnly:
Residents of Madhya Pradesh live under the national framework with no provincial statute addressing transgender recognition, and an estimated two million transgender people live across the country.

For residents seeking gender-affirming surgery, the March 2026 amendment makes certification by a medical board and the district authority mandatory, and legal recognition itself is conditioned on medical certification rather than self-declaration.

Residents who self-identify outside the historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex category fall outside the recognition scheme, which affects access to welfare schemes, education and employment protections that depend on recognised status.

Residents face the same criminal-law position: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force since 2024, dropped the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence under the Indian Penal Code, and communities report fear of more assaults. Same-sex acts have been decriminalised since 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex as interpreted to cover gender identity.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are unavailable to residents, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. Residents also face the new offences for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, which People's Union for Civil Liberties says echo colonial-era criminalisation, and activist Akkai Padmashali describes the amendment as an attack on the right to exist.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was still pending at the time of sourcing; whether it has since been assented to, and on what date, is unresolved here.

No Madhya Pradesh-specific enforcement data, police conduct reports, facility access records or state government positions on the amendment are sourced for this record.

Whether certificates and identity documents already issued to trans people in Madhya Pradesh under the 2019 self-identification route remain valid after the amendment, and whether any transition period applies, is not sourced.

Whether Madhya Pradesh police have adopted sensitisation directives, conversion-therapy bans or the kind of guidelines issued by the Madras High Court in 2021 is not sourced.

Whether the amendment's certification requirements apply to foreign visitors presenting documents issued abroad, as opposed to Indian applicants, is not addressed in the sources.
